items.title: Integrated Judiciary & the Supreme Court
items.body:
## In one line

India has one single chain of courts, with the **Supreme Court** at the top, that applies both Union and State laws.

## Why it is asked

Examiners test the 'integrated' idea (how it differs from the US dual system), the Supreme Court's start date and strength, and the appointment and removal of judges.

## The story

Before 1950 the highest court in British India was the **Federal Court of India**, set up under the Government of India Act, 1935. When the Constitution came into force on 26 January 1950, this was replaced by the **Supreme Court of India**, which held its first sitting on **28 January 1950** — two days later.

The framers chose a **single integrated judiciary**: one pyramid of courts — **Supreme Court → High Courts → subordinate (district) courts** — where the same courts enforce central laws and state laws alike. This is unlike the United States, where federal and state courts run as two separate systems. The aim was to keep the law uniform across the whole country and let appeals flow upward to one apex court.

The Supreme Court is covered in **Part V, Chapter IV, Articles 124-147**. It began in 1950 with only **8 judges** (including the Chief Justice). As the workload grew, Parliament raised the number several times; since **2019 the sanctioned strength is 34 judges** — the Chief Justice of India plus 33 others.

To become a Supreme Court judge (Article 124) a person must be an Indian citizen and have either **5 years as a High Court judge**, or **10 years as a High Court advocate**, or be a **distinguished jurist** in the President's opinion. The Constitution fixes **no minimum age**. Judges are appointed by the **President** acting on the recommendation of the **Collegium** (the Chief Justice of India and the four senior-most judges). An attempt to replace the Collegium with a government-involved body — the National Judicial Appointments Commission (99th Amendment) — was **struck down by the Supreme Court in 2015**.

A Supreme Court judge retires at **65** and can be removed only for **proven misbehaviour or incapacity**, through the hard process in **Article 124(4)** (a special majority in each House of Parliament, backed by the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968).

## Why it matters

A single apex court sitting above every other court is what makes constitutional law uniform and gives citizens one final forum — the base of judicial independence and judicial review.

## Terms explained

- **Integrated judiciary** — one connected set of courts (not separate central and state systems).
- **Collegium** — the group of senior judges (Chief Justice + 4) that recommends who becomes a judge.
- **Sanctioned strength** — the maximum number of judges a court is allowed to have.
- **Special majority (Article 124(4))** — a majority of the total membership of a House plus two-thirds of the members present and voting.
- **Jurist** — a legal expert or scholar of law.

## Don't confuse

| Point | Supreme Court | High Court |
|---|---|---|
| Retirement age | 65 years | 62 years |
| Constitutional location | Part V (124-147) | Part VI (214-231) |

## Remember it

'Senior Court is older': the **S**upreme Court retires at **65**, the **H**igh Court at **62** (65 > 62).

## TL;DR

- One integrated judiciary: Supreme Court → High Courts → subordinate courts; same courts apply Union and State law.
- Supreme Court first sat on **28 January 1950**; successor to the Federal Court (1935 Act); Part V, Articles 124-147.
- Sanctioned strength **34** (began with 8); Parliament fixes the number under Article 124.
- Judges appointed by the President via the **Collegium**; NJAC struck down in **2015**.
- Retire at **65**; removed only for proven misbehaviour or incapacity by special majority (Article 124(4)).
keyPoints: Single integrated judiciary, three-tier: Supreme Court > High Courts > Subordinate Courts.
Supreme Court inaugurated 28 January 1950; successor to the Federal Court (GoI Act 1935).
Covered by Part V, Articles 124-147; present strength 34 judges (originally 8).
SC judge qualifications: 5 years as HC judge OR 10 years as HC advocate; no minimum age.
Judges appointed by the President via the Collegium; NJAC struck down in 2015.
SC judges retire at 65; removed under Article 124(4) by special majority (Judges Inquiry Act 1968).
items.mnemonic: SC age 65, HC age 62 — 'Senior Court is older' (65 > 62).

items.title: Jurisdiction & Powers of the Supreme Court
items.body:
## In one line

The Supreme Court has several different 'doors' through which a case can reach it — original, writ, appellate, special-leave and advisory — plus special powers to bind all courts and do complete justice.

## Why it is asked

Matching the right Article to the right power (131 / 32 / 136 / 143 / 141 / 142) is one of the most common Polity question types.

## The story

'Jurisdiction' simply means the kinds of cases a court is allowed to hear. The Supreme Court has five main heads of jurisdiction, each tied to an Article.

| Type | Article | Scope |
|---|---|---|
| Original | 131 | Centre-State and inter-State disputes (exclusive — the case starts here) |
| Writ | 32 | Enforcement of Fundamental Rights; five writs |
| Appellate | 132 / 133 / 134 | Constitutional, civil and criminal appeals |
| Special Leave | 136 | Discretionary appeal from any court or tribunal (except military) |
| Advisory | 143 | President refers a question of law or fact; the opinion is not binding |

Beyond hearing cases, the Court has powers that shape the whole legal system. **Article 141** makes the law it declares **binding on all courts** in India. **Article 142** lets it pass any order needed for **complete justice** (used in matters such as Ayodhya and the Bhopal gas case). **Article 137** lets it **review its own judgments**. Through **judicial review** it can strike down any law or executive act that breaks the Constitution — a power held to be part of the **basic structure**. The rise of **Public Interest Litigation (PIL)** relaxed the old rule that only an affected person could sue, widening access to justice.

Under its writ jurisdiction (Article 32) the Court issues **five writs**: **Habeas Corpus** (produce the detained person), **Mandamus** (command a public authority to do its duty), **Prohibition** (stop a lower court exceeding its powers, before it acts), **Certiorari** (quash an order already passed) and **Quo Warranto** (question a person's right to hold a public office).

## Why it matters

These heads decide where a dispute must begin and how far the Court can go — the practical machinery behind phrases like 'guardian of the Constitution'.

## Terms explained

- **Original jurisdiction** — the case is filed and heard first in that court, not on appeal.
- **Writ** — a formal written court order directing someone to act or stop acting.
- **Special Leave Petition (SLP)** — a request asking the Court to use its discretion to hear an appeal; it is a favour, not a right.
- **Advisory jurisdiction** — the Court gives an opinion (not a binding verdict) when the President asks.
- **Locus standi** — the right to bring a case; PIL relaxed it.

## Don't confuse

| Power | Article | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| Binding precedent | 141 | SC's law binds all courts |
| Complete justice | 142 | Any order to do justice |
| Review | 137 | Re-examine its own ruling |

## Remember it

Writs spell **'HM-PCQ'**: **H**abeas Corpus, **M**andamus, **P**rohibition, **C**ertiorari, **Q**uo Warranto.

## TL;DR

- Original (131) = Centre-State and inter-State disputes.
- Writ (32) = enforce Fundamental Rights (Ambedkar: 'heart and soul'); five writs HM-PCQ.
- Special Leave (136) = widest discretionary appeal (not for military tribunals); Advisory (143) = non-binding opinion.
- Article 141 binds all courts; Article 142 allows orders for complete justice; Article 137 is review.
- Judicial review is part of the basic structure; PIL widened access to justice.
keyPoints: Original jurisdiction (Art 131) covers Centre-State and inter-State disputes.
Writ jurisdiction under Art 32 enforces Fundamental Rights (Ambedkar: 'heart and soul').
Article 136 = Special Leave Petition, the widest discretionary appellate power (not for military tribunals).
Article 143 = advisory jurisdiction; the opinion is not binding on the President.
Article 141 makes SC law binding on all courts; Article 142 allows orders for complete justice.
Five writs: Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, Quo Warranto.
items.mnemonic: Writs 'HM-PCQ': Habeas, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, Quo Warranto.

items.title: High Courts — Provisions & Jurisdiction
items.body:
## In one line

Each State normally has a **High Court** — the top court of the State — with a writ power that is actually wider than the Supreme Court's.

## Why it is asked

The Article numbers (214-231), the 'wider than Article 32' point and the appointment/transfer rules are repeatedly tested.

## The story

The first three High Courts were created in **1862** at **Calcutta, Bombay and Madras** under the Indian High Courts Act, 1861. Today India has **25 High Courts**. Normally there is one High Court per State, but the **Seventh Amendment Act, 1956** allowed Parliament to set up a **common High Court** for two or more States or Union Territories (Article 231).

The constitutional scheme runs through **Articles 214-231**: **214** — a High Court for each State; **215** — the High Court is a court of record; **216** — it has a Chief Justice and other judges; **217** — appointment and service conditions; **222** — transfer of a judge from one High Court to another; **226** — the writ power; **227** — superintendence over courts below it; **231** — common High Court.

High Court judges are appointed by the **President**. For judges other than the Chief Justice, the President consults the **Chief Justice of India, the State Governor and the Chief Justice of that High Court**. A candidate must be an Indian citizen with either **10 years of judicial office** or **10 years as a High Court advocate**. A High Court judge retires at **62** and can be removed only by the **President on an address by both Houses of Parliament** for proven misbehaviour or incapacity — the same tough process as for Supreme Court judges. Transfer of a judge is done by the President under **Article 222** after consulting the Chief Justice of India.

The standout feature is **Article 226**: a High Court can issue writs **both for Fundamental Rights and for 'any other purpose'** (any legal right). Because Article 32 of the Supreme Court is limited to Fundamental Rights only, the High Court's writ jurisdiction is **wider in subject matter** — though it runs only within the High Court's own territory.

## Why it matters

Most citizens reach the courts first through a High Court writ under Article 226, so its wider scope is of real practical importance.

## Terms explained

- **Court of record** — a court whose judgments are recorded as permanent evidence and which can punish for contempt.
- **Superintendence (Article 227)** — supervisory control over all lower courts and tribunals in the area.
- **'For any other purpose'** — the extra phrase in Article 226 that lets a High Court protect ordinary legal rights, not just Fundamental Rights.
- **Transfer (Article 222)** — moving a sitting judge from one High Court to another.

## Don't confuse

| Point | Article 32 (SC) | Article 226 (HC) |
|---|---|---|
| Covers | Fundamental Rights only | FRs + 'any other purpose' |
| Reach | Whole of India | That State's territory |
| Status | Itself a Fundamental Right | A constitutional right |

## Remember it

High Court writs are **'wider but local'**: Article 226 covers more grounds, but only inside the State.

## TL;DR

- High Court Articles 214-231; first three (1862): Calcutta, Bombay, Madras; India has 25 High Courts.
- Seventh Amendment 1956 allows a common High Court for two or more States (Article 231).
- Judges appointed by the President (consulting CJI, Governor, HC Chief Justice); qualification 10 years' judicial office or advocacy.
- Retire at 62; removed by the President on a parliamentary address; transfer under Article 222.
- Article 226 (writs 'for any other purpose') is wider than Article 32; Article 227 = superintendence.
keyPoints: High Court Articles: 214-231; first HCs (1862) at Calcutta, Bombay, Madras.
India has 25 High Courts; Seventh Amendment 1956 allows a common HC for two+ States.
HC judges appointed by the President consulting CJI, Governor and HC Chief Justice.
HC judge qualification: 10 years' judicial office OR 10 years as an HC advocate.
HC judges retire at 62; removal by President on a parliamentary address.
Article 226 (writs 'for any other purpose') is wider than Article 32; Article 227 = superintendence.
items.mnemonic: HC writs are 'wider' — Art 226 covers FRs + 'any other purpose'; Art 32 is FR-only.

items.title: High Court of Andhra Pradesh (Amaravati)
items.body:
## In one line

Andhra Pradesh got its own separate High Court at **Amaravati on 1 January 2019**, carved out of the common High Court at Hyderabad.

## Why it is asked

This is a direct AP-angle fact: date, seat, and the twin-court split with Telangana are easy one-mark questions.

## The story

When Andhra Pradesh was bifurcated in 2014 to create Telangana, the two new States shared one court — the **High Court of Judicature at Hyderabad** — as a **common High Court**. This was only a temporary arrangement under the **Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act, 2014**.

A separate **High Court of Andhra Pradesh** was then created by a **Presidential order that took effect on 1 January 2019**. Its seat is at **Amaravati (Nelapadu)**, in the State's capital region. The common court at Hyderabad continued, from the same date, as the **Telangana High Court**. So two High Courts — AP (Amaravati) and Telangana (Hyderabad) — both date their separate existence from 2019.

From 2019 the AP High Court exercises full **writ jurisdiction under Article 226** for the whole State. Below it sits the Andhra Pradesh district judiciary, where **District Judges are appointed by the Governor in consultation with the High Court** under **Article 233**.

## Why it matters

It is the newest big change to AP's judicial map and a favourite 'current + static' crossover question in APPSC Polity.

## Terms explained

- **Bifurcation** — splitting one State (or one court) into two.
- **Common High Court** — a single High Court serving two States at once (allowed by Article 231).
- **Presidential order** — a formal notification issued by the President to give effect to a reorganisation.
- **Seat** — the official location where a court sits (here, Amaravati-Nelapadu).

## Don't confuse

| Court | Seat | Separate since |
|---|---|---|
| Andhra Pradesh HC | Amaravati (Nelapadu) | 1 January 2019 |
| Telangana HC | Hyderabad | 1 January 2019 |

## Remember it

**'Amaravati, 1-1-2019'** — New Year, new court.

## TL;DR

- AP High Court created by Presidential order effective 1 January 2019 under the AP Reorganisation Act, 2014.
- Seat: Amaravati (Nelapadu), the State's capital region.
- Bifurcated from the common High Court at Hyderabad, which became the Telangana High Court.
- Both the AP and Telangana High Courts date their separate existence from 2019.
- It exercises Article 226 writ jurisdiction for the whole State.
keyPoints: AP High Court created by Presidential order effective 1 January 2019 under the AP Reorganisation Act, 2014.
Seat is Amaravati (Nelapadu), Andhra Pradesh's capital region.
It was bifurcated from the common High Court at Hyderabad, which became the Telangana High Court.
Both the AP (Amaravati) and Telangana (Hyderabad) High Courts date from 2019.
The AP High Court exercises Article 226 writ jurisdiction for the whole State.

items.title: Subordinate Courts (Articles 233-237)
items.body:
## In one line

Below the High Court sit the **district and lower courts**, headed by the District & Sessions Judge, plus people-friendly forums like Lok Adalats and Gram Nyayalayas.

## Why it is asked

Who appoints District Judges (Article 233), the civil-criminal hierarchy, and the free-legal-aid bodies are frequent one-mark and statement questions.

## The story

The lowest tier of the judiciary is governed by **Articles 233-237**. Under **Article 233** the **Governor appoints District Judges in consultation with the High Court** — a candidate needs 7 years as an advocate and must not already be in government service. **Article 234** covers recruitment of judicial officers below District Judge, done by the Governor with the **State Public Service Commission** and the High Court. **Article 235** gives the High Court **control** over postings, promotions and leave of the district judiciary. **Article 236** clarifies that 'District Judge' includes the Sessions Judge, Additional Sessions Judge and Chief Judicial Magistrate.

The courts are arranged in two ladders:

| Side | Higher → Lower |
|---|---|
| Civil | District/Subordinate Judge → Munsiff → Small Causes |
| Criminal | Sessions Court → CJM (up to 7 years) → JM First Class (up to 3 years) → Second Class |

The **same officer** acts as the **District Judge** on the civil side and the **Sessions Judge** on the criminal side. An important safeguard: a **death sentence** passed by a Sessions Court must be **confirmed by the High Court** before it can be carried out.

To widen access to justice, **NALSA** (the National Legal Services Authority) was created under the **Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987**, giving effect to **Article 39A** (a Directive Principle promising free legal aid). NALSA organises **Lok Adalats**, whose awards are **final and non-appealable** and carry the status of a civil-court decree. **Gram Nyayalayas**, set up under an Act of **2008**, are **mobile courts** that take justice to the village level, handling both civil and criminal cases.

## Why it matters

Most ordinary cases live and die in these courts; the legal-aid machinery is how the Constitution's promise of 'justice for all' reaches poor litigants.

## Terms explained

- **Munsiff** — the lowest civil judge in a district.
- **Sessions Court** — the court that tries serious criminal offences.
- **CJM / JMFC** — Chief Judicial Magistrate / Judicial Magistrate First Class (criminal magistrates with limited sentencing powers).
- **Lok Adalat** — a 'people's court' that settles disputes by compromise; its award is final.
- **Gram Nyayalaya** — a mobile village court (2008 Act).
- **Article 39A** — a Directive Principle requiring the State to provide free legal aid.

## Don't confuse

| Court | Role |
|---|---|
| District Judge | Highest civil court in the district |
| Munsiff | Lowest civil court |
| Sessions Court | Can award death penalty (HC must confirm) |
| CJM | Imprisonment up to 7 years, not death |

## Remember it

**'39A + Act 1987 = NALSA'** — free legal aid; a **Lok Adalat award is final**.

## TL;DR

- Subordinate courts: Articles 233-237; District Judges appointed by the Governor with the High Court (Article 233).
- Article 235 gives the High Court control over the district judiciary.
- Civil: District/Subordinate Judge > Munsiff; Criminal: Sessions Court > CJM (up to 7 years) > JMFC (up to 3 years).
- A death sentence by a Sessions Court needs High Court confirmation.
- NALSA (1987 Act) serves Article 39A and runs Lok Adalats; Lok Adalat awards are final; Gram Nyayalayas (2008) are rural mobile courts.
keyPoints: Subordinate courts: Articles 233-237; District Judges appointed by the Governor with the High Court (Art 233).
Article 235 gives the High Court control over the district judiciary.
Civil hierarchy: District/Subordinate Judge > Munsiff; Criminal: Sessions Court > CJM (<=7 yrs) > JMFC (<=3 yrs).
A death sentence by a Sessions Court needs High Court confirmation.
NALSA (LSA Act 1987) gives effect to Article 39A and runs Lok Adalats.
Lok Adalat awards are final and non-appealable; Gram Nyayalayas (2008) are rural mobile courts.
items.mnemonic: Article 39A + Act 1987 = NALSA free legal aid; Lok Adalat award = final.

items.title: Judicial Independence, Review & Landmark Cases
items.body:
## In one line

The Constitution protects judges from pressure so they can freely strike down unconstitutional laws — a power sharpened by a handful of landmark cases.

## Why it is asked

The safeguards list, the meaning of judicial review and the famous cases (Kesavananda, Maneka Gandhi, Vishaka, Bommai) are staple Polity material for both Prelims and Mains.

## The story

For courts to act fairly, judges must be free from fear and favour. The Constitution builds in several **safeguards for independence**. Judges have **security of tenure** — they can be removed only for proven misbehaviour or incapacity, through a hard impeachment-like process. They have **financial security** — salaries are charged on the Consolidated Fund and cannot be reduced to a judge's disadvantage (except in a financial emergency). There is **separation from the executive** (urged by Directive Principle Article 50), a **ban on practice after retirement** for Supreme Court judges, a bar on discussing a judge's conduct in the legislature, and **contempt powers** to protect the court's authority.

The sharpest tool is **judicial review** — the power to declare a law or executive act void if it violates the Constitution. This power is itself part of the **basic structure** and cannot be taken away. The spread of **Public Interest Litigation (PIL)** widened who may approach the court, raising the debate of **judicial activism** (courts stepping in to protect rights) versus **judicial restraint** (leaving policy to elected organs).

A few landmark cases map how the Court used these powers:

| Case | Contribution |
|---|---|
| Kesavananda Bharati (1973) | Basic structure doctrine |
| Golaknath (1967) | Fundamental Rights held unamendable (later modified) |
| Maneka Gandhi (1978) | Expanded Article 21 (due process) |
| Vishaka (1997) | Guidelines against workplace sexual harassment |
| S. R. Bommai (1994) | Curbed misuse of Article 356 |

## Why it matters

These protections and cases are why the judiciary can check the other two organs — the heart of 'checks and balances' in India.

## Terms explained

- **Judicial review** — courts testing laws and acts against the Constitution and invalidating those that fail.
- **Basic structure** — the core features (like democracy, judicial review, federalism) that even a constitutional amendment cannot destroy.
- **PIL** — a case filed in the public interest, where strict standing rules are relaxed.
- **Judicial activism vs restraint** — how far courts should enter the policy space.
- **Consolidated Fund** — the government's main account; charging salaries on it keeps them outside yearly political voting.

## Don't confuse

| Case | What it is famous for |
|---|---|
| Kesavananda Bharati (1973) | Basic structure |
| Maneka Gandhi (1978) | Wider Article 21 |
| S. R. Bommai (1994) | Limits on Article 356 |

## Remember it

**'Basic structure = Kesavananda 1973; Article 21 grows = Maneka 1978.'**

## TL;DR

- Independence rests on security of tenure, protected salaries, separation from the executive (Article 50) and contempt powers.
- Judicial review lets courts strike down unconstitutional laws and is part of the basic structure.
- PIL relaxed standing rules and expanded access to justice.
- Kesavananda Bharati (1973) = basic structure; Maneka Gandhi (1978) = wider Article 21.
- Vishaka (1997) = anti-harassment guidelines; S. R. Bommai (1994) = curbed Article 356 misuse.
keyPoints: Independence safeguards: security of tenure, protected salaries, separation from executive (Art 50), contempt powers.
Judicial review lets courts strike down unconstitutional laws; it is part of the basic structure.
PIL relaxed locus standi and expanded access to justice.
Kesavananda Bharati (1973) laid down the basic structure doctrine.
Maneka Gandhi (1978) expanded Article 21; Vishaka (1997) set anti-harassment guidelines.
items.mnemonic: Basic structure = Kesavananda 1973; Art 21 expansion = Maneka 1978.

items.title: Andhra Pradesh Judiciary — High Court & District Courts (2026)
items.body:
## In one line

A current-affairs snapshot of the AP judiciary: the High Court at Amaravati, its strength and Chief Justice, the district courts, and the State legal-aid body.

## Why it is asked

APPSC loves 'as of today' AP facts — strength, the sitting Chief Justice, and who heads legal aid.

## The story

The **High Court of Andhra Pradesh** began functioning on **1 January 2019** with its seat at **Amaravati (Nelapadu)**, after being bifurcated from the common High Court at Hyderabad (which stayed on as the Telangana High Court). Its **sanctioned strength is 37 judges** — made up of **28 permanent and 9 additional** judges. As of **September 2026** the **Chief Justice is Justice Lisa Gill**, who was sworn in on **25 April 2026**.

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| Started functioning | 1 January 2019 |
| Seat | Amaravati (Nelapadu) |
| Origin | Bifurcated from the common High Court at Hyderabad |
| Sanctioned strength | 37 judges (28 permanent + 9 additional) |
| Chief Justice (Sep 2026) | Justice Lisa Gill (sworn in 25 April 2026) |

Below the High Court, **District Judges are appointed by the Governor in consultation with the High Court (Article 233)**; other judicial-service posts fall under **Article 234**, and the High Court exercises **control over subordinate courts (Article 235)**. The district tier runs from the **District & Sessions Court** down through Senior and Junior Civil Judge courts and the Chief Judicial / Judicial Magistrate courts.

For free legal aid, the **AP State Legal Services Authority (APSLSA)** functions under the **Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987** (giving effect to Article 39A). Its **Patron-in-Chief is the Chief Justice of the AP High Court**, and the **Lok Adalat** awards it organises are **final and non-appealable**, with the status of a civil-court decree.

## Why it matters

These are the exact figures and names an examiner can lift straight into a one-mark question, so they must be current.

## Terms explained

- **Permanent judge** — a judge appointed for the full term up to retirement.
- **Additional judge** — appointed for a fixed period (up to two years) to clear extra workload.
- **Patron-in-Chief** — the ceremonial head of a legal-services authority (here, the Chief Justice).
- **APSLSA** — Andhra Pradesh State Legal Services Authority.

## Don't confuse

| Figure | Value |
|---|---|
| AP HC sanctioned strength | 37 (28 permanent + 9 additional) |
| Supreme Court strength | 34 (do not mix the two) |

## Remember it

**'37 = 28 + 9'** for the AP High Court; the Chief Justice (2026) is **Lisa Gill**.

## TL;DR

- AP High Court started 1 January 2019 at Amaravati (Nelapadu); sanctioned strength 37 (28 permanent + 9 additional).
- Chief Justice as of September 2026: Justice Lisa Gill (sworn in 25 April 2026).
- Carved out of the common Hyderabad High Court; Telangana kept the Hyderabad court.
- District Judges appointed by the Governor with the High Court (Article 233); HC controls subordinate courts (Article 235).
- APSLSA runs under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987; the CJ of the AP HC is its Patron-in-Chief; Lok Adalat awards are final.
keyPoints: AP High Court started 1 Jan 2019 at Amaravati (Nelapadu); sanctioned strength 37 judges (28 permanent + 9 additional)
Chief Justice of AP High Court as of Sep 2026: Justice Lisa Gill (sworn in 25 April 2026)
AP HC was carved out of the common Hyderabad High Court; Telangana retained the Hyderabad court
District Judges appointed by the Governor with HC consultation (Art 233); HC controls subordinate courts (Art 235)
APSLSA under Legal Services Authorities Act 1987; CJ of AP HC is Patron-in-Chief; Lok Adalat awards are final

items.title: Bar Councils, Custody, Writ Scope & Article 128
items.body:
## In one line

Four smaller but exam-worthy points: who regulates lawyers, the two kinds of custody, the limits of two writs, and the recall of a retired judge.

## Why it is asked

These appear as statement-based (1-and-2) questions where one wrong word flips the answer.

## The story

**Bar Council of India (Advocates Act, 1961).** The Bar Council of India lays down the **standards of legal education**, recognises law degrees and controls the **enrolment of advocates**. The University Grants Commission regulates higher education generally, but not who may practise law.

**Judicial custody versus police custody.** In **police custody** the accused is held in a **police lock-up** so the police can question them. In **judicial custody** the accused is lodged in **jail**, and the police **cannot interrogate without the magistrate's permission**.

**Scope of two writs.** A **Mandamus** commands a public authority to perform a public duty — so it does **not** lie against a purely **private body with no public duty**. A **Quo Warranto** questions a person's right to hold a public office and can be sought by **any person**, not only the one directly aggrieved.

**Article 128.** The **Chief Justice of India, with the President's prior consent**, may request a **retired Supreme Court judge** to sit and act again as a judge of the Supreme Court — useful when extra hands are needed.

## Why it matters

Each point is a classic 'trap' detail: the exam flips 'public' to 'private', or 'any person' to 'aggrieved person', to test precision.

## Terms explained

- **Enrolment** — formal registration that lets a person practise as an advocate.
- **Interrogation** — formal questioning of an accused by the police.
- **Public duty** — a legal obligation owed by a public authority (what Mandamus enforces).
- **Quo Warranto** — Latin for 'by what authority'; challenges a wrongful office-holder.

## Don't confuse

| Point | Correct position |
|---|---|
| Police custody | Police lock-up, for interrogation |
| Judicial custody | Jail; no interrogation without magistrate's leave |
| Mandamus | Public duty only, not a private body |
| Quo Warranto | Any person may seek it |

## Remember it

**'Private = no Mandamus; Any person = Quo Warranto; CJI + President = recall (Article 128).'**

## TL;DR

- The Bar Council of India (Advocates Act 1961) sets standards of legal education and controls enrolment.
- Police custody = police lock-up for interrogation; judicial custody = jail, no interrogation without the magistrate's permission.
- Mandamus does not lie against a private body with no public duty; Quo Warranto can be sought by any person.
- Article 128 lets the CJI, with the President's consent, recall a retired Supreme Court judge.
keyPoints: The Bar Council of India (Advocates Act 1961) sets standards of legal education and controls enrolment.
Police custody = police lock-up for interrogation; judicial custody = jail, no interrogation without magistrate's permission.
Mandamus does not lie against a private body with no public duty; Quo Warranto can be sought by any person.
Article 128 lets the CJI, with the President's consent, recall a retired Supreme Court judge.

items.title: For Mains — The Judiciary
items.body:
The judiciary clause in **GS Paper-3 (mains-3)** — 'Judiciary: structure, emergency, amendments, judicial review, PIL' (and the civil/criminal-law clause) — is answered best analytically, not as a list of Articles. Pick the dimensions the question asks and build a crisp table.

| Dimension | Content to deploy |
|---|---|
| Structure | Integrated three-tier judiciary; SC (Part V), HCs (Part VI), subordinate courts (233-237) |
| Independence | Security of tenure, salaries on Consolidated Fund, Collegium primacy, contempt powers |
| Judicial review | Part of the basic structure (Kesavananda, 1973); checks legislature and executive |
| Activism vs overreach | PIL expanded access; concern when courts enter the policy domain |
| Appointments debate | Collegium (Second & Third Judges Cases) vs NJAC struck down (2015); opacity vs accountability |
| Reform / way forward | Transparent Memorandum of Procedure, All-India Judicial Service, pendency and vacancies, judicial infrastructure |

**Data points and authorities to quote:** basic structure doctrine — *Kesavananda Bharati* (1973); expansion of Article 21 — *Maneka Gandhi* (1978); NJAC struck down 4:1 (2015); *S. R. Bommai* (1994) on Article 356; the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968; large case pendency (crores of pending cases across courts) and persistent High Court vacancies as governance challenges; the 2nd Administrative Reforms Commission on access to justice.

**AP angle:** the AP High Court at Amaravati (2019, strength 37) and the AP State Legal Services Authority show how a young High Court builds capacity; Lok Adalats and Gram Nyayalayas illustrate access-to-justice reform at the grassroots.

**Use in answers:**
- *Example:* contrast the Collegium's opacity with the 2015 NJAC verdict to argue for a transparent-but-independent model.
- *Quote:* Ambedkar called Article 32 the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution — use it to frame judicial review.
- *Diagram idea:* a 'golden triangle' linking Articles 14, 19 and 21, or a three-tier court pyramid, to open the answer visually.

Conclude by linking an independent, accessible judiciary to constitutional morality and the rule of law.
keyPoints: Frame judiciary answers around dimensions (structure, independence, review, activism, appointments, reform) — not an Article list.
Anchor with Kesavananda (1973), Maneka Gandhi (1978), NJAC struck down (2015), S. R. Bommai (1994).
Appointments debate: Collegium primacy vs transparency; way forward is a clear Memorandum of Procedure and filling vacancies.
Cite pendency and High Court vacancies as the core access-to-justice challenge.
AP angle: AP High Court (Amaravati, 2019, strength 37), APSLSA, Lok Adalats and Gram Nyayalayas.
Open with the Article 32 'heart and soul' quote or a three-tier/golden-triangle diagram; close on rule of law.
